claims.text: The proposed intervention is to add 1–3 wt.% tungsten or tantalum during initial alloy melting or processing.
Adding 1–3 wt.% tungsten or tantalum will promote the formation and uniform dispersion of sigma-phase particles.
Sigma-phase particles obstruct dislocation motion and grain-boundary motion.
The baseline refractory high-entropy alloy has a coarse or uneven sigma-phase distribution.
The baseline refractory high-entropy alloy has limited elevated-temperature ductility.
The intervention will produce a refined, uniformly dispersed population of sigma-phase particles along grain boundaries and within grains.
The added tungsten or tantalum will promote sigma-phase nucleation and stabilization.
Sigma-phase particles act as pinning centers for dislocations and impede grain-boundary migration.
The proposed pinning mechanism will reduce localized strain concentration.
The proposed pinning mechanism will delay intergranular fracture at high temperature.
Relative to the alloy without the refractory addition, the modified alloy will have greater tensile fracture strain at elevated temperature.
Relative to the alloy without the refractory addition, the modified alloy will have greater creep rupture life at elevated temperature.
The improvement in elevated-temperature tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life could exceed twofold.
Baseline alloys without the addition are prone to grain-boundary sliding and intergranular cracking at high temperature.
The predicted improvement should be observable around 650°C under high-stress tensile and creep loading.
Effects outside the stated thermal regime or at substantially different deformation rates are unverified.
The optimal tungsten or tantalum concentration within the 1–3 wt.% range is uncertain.
Different base-alloy compositions may change the magnitude of the predicted improvement.
